producerBrief:
TEMPO / KEY / FEEL: 112 BPM, 4/4, D major, big steady stomp. Anthemic, bittersweet and wide open, like the last scene of a film.

VOICE: Dramatic male baritone who starts in a low, intimate croon, cracks into a higher, urgent shout on the chorus, and half-speaks the breakdown. Slightly theatrical with a breathy edge. Crowd-style gang vocals on every 'na-na' chant, as if a whole school is singing.

INSTRUMENTS: Big, booming drums with a tom-heavy pattern and a huge gated-reverb snare (the heartbeat). An octave-pulsing bass line. Chiming electric guitar soaked in delay, playing ringing two-note shapes. Bright, glassy synth chords and a sustained organ pad. A sparkling keyboard counter-melody in the chorus. Tambourine on the backbeat.

ARRANGEMENT MAP: 0:00 Intro, a crashing drum fill and the gang 'na-na' chant twice over full band. 0:17 Verse 1, drums, bass and low croon, guitar chiming in the gaps. 0:51 Chorus 1, full band, the voice jumps an octave. 1:17 Verse 2. 1:51 Chorus 2. 2:17 Instrumental, delayed guitar and synth trading phrases. 2:34 Breakdown, everything out except kick, bass and the half-spoken vocal. 2:51 Build, the chant returns one voice at a time, a snare roll growing under it for 8 bars. 3:08 Final chorus at full power with ad-libs. 3:34 Outro, the chant repeating over the full band with shouted answers, slowly fading with the crowd still singing at 4:20.

PRODUCTION & MIX: Huge and reverberant. Drums like they were recorded in a gymnasium, guitars and synths wide, vocal dry in the verses then echoing in the chorus.

SIGNATURE MOMENT: The breakdown and rebuild. One low voice, then the chant returning voice by voice until the whole room has its fist in the air.

MODERN POINT OF VIEW: The gang vocals are layered like a modern stadium crowd, with real handclaps. The low end is fuller and the fade is long, designed for a film's end credits.

EMOTIONAL ARC: Vulnerable, insistent, then communal and defiant.

WHAT IT IS ABOUT

A Saturday that made two nobodies feel like somebody, and the fear of Monday. Decades later one of them hears four notes in an elevator and is seventeen again. The request: don't remember me politely.

THE OTHER WAYS TO HEAR IT

Hear it as: a graduation or reunion anthem; a break-up song; a message from a friend who died young; a parent speaking to a grown child; or the 1980s themselves talking to the people who lived them. 'Loud' is sung so it also sounds like 'aloud' and 'allowed': say my name out loud, and let me be remembered.

ENGINEERED HOOKS AND THE DESIGNED MISHEARING

Borrowed mechanics: questions in the verses, a plea in the chorus, a chant anyone can join after one hearing, and a breakdown that rebuilds from drums and bass. The lanyard-and-parking-space verse is aimed squarely at the grown-up 80s kid. Designed mishearing: loud / aloud / allowed, plus 'Remember me, Lloyd', which someone will insist is the real lyric.
